questions.q: What does risk parity target, in contrast to an equal-dollar-weight portfolio?
options: Equal risk CONTRIBUTION from each asset, not equal dollar allocation
The exact same thing as equal-weight -- the two are mathematically identical
Maximizing expected return regardless of risk
Minimizing the number of assets held
questions.explain: An equal-dollar-weight portfolio is not balanced in risk terms if assets have different volatilities; risk parity specifically targets equal risk contribution from each asset.

questions.q: In the worked example (vols = [0.15, 0.20, 0.25]), why does the least volatile asset get the LARGEST inverse-volatility weight (42.55%)?
options: Inverse-volatility weighting allocates more to lower-volatility assets specifically to equalize each asset's contribution to overall risk
Lower-volatility assets always have higher expected returns
This is an error -- all assets should get equal weight
The lowest-volatility asset is always the best investment
questions.explain: Weighting inversely to volatility means the least volatile asset gets the biggest allocation, which is exactly what makes w_i * vol_i come out equal (0.0638) across all three assets.

questions.q: What does inverse-volatility weighting ignore that a full, correlation-aware risk-parity solution would account for?
options: Correlations between assets -- it treats each asset's risk contribution as if it existed in isolation
Volatility -- it ignores volatility entirely
The number of assets in the portfolio
Nothing -- inverse-volatility weighting is already the exact full solution
questions.explain: Inverse-volatility weighting is a simplified approximation that ignores correlation; the full risk-parity solution requires solving a nonlinear system accounting for every covariance term.

questions.q: What is risk parity's biggest structural advantage over the mean-variance framework from Lesson 36?
options: It requires no expected-return estimate at all, avoiding the hardest, least stable input in mean-variance optimization
It always produces higher returns than mean-variance
It requires inverting a larger matrix, which is more accurate
It eliminates the need for a covariance matrix
questions.explain: Risk parity depends only on volatilities (and, in the full version, correlations) -- never on expected returns, which is the single hardest input to estimate reliably in Lesson 36's mean-variance framework.

questions.q: What is the real cost of risk parity's independence from expected-return forecasts?
options: It has no mechanism to act on a genuine, validated view that one asset should outperform another
It cannot be computed without a supercomputer
It only works for exactly two assets
It requires more historical data than mean-variance optimization
questions.explain: By design, risk parity ignores expected returns entirely -- so even a well-validated view that one asset should outperform has no way to influence the resulting weights.
